record.tranche_reason: The study directly tests grokking-related behaviour under different example orderings and argues that, in its modular-arithmetic setting, IID ordering contributes to the delay while fixed ordering can remove it. It also reports a different account of how the generalizing representation forms.
record.gate_note: The study’s own modular-arithmetic accuracy, spectral, gradient, seed-sweep, and weight-decay results are included. Results cited from other work, such as GraB results on CIFAR-10, WikiText, and GLUE, are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study's own modular-addition runs (p = 9973, 0.3% data) report train/test trajectories, Fourier spectra, spectral entropy and a layer-level progress measure under four example orderings. On that basis it argues the grokking delay is, in this domain, an artifact of IID ordering. Those results bear on V1, V2, V5 and V6. V7 names optimizer or numerical artifacts, not data ordering, so the ordering argument is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with one addition. The authors state that in this domain the grokking delay is 'an artifact of IID data ordering' that structured ordering eliminates entirely, and that ordering is a major contributor in SGD-trained models generally; they deny it is a universal explanation. Their own Section 5.1.1 still shows a ~90% train-test gap under fixed ordering, which they reinterpret as underdetermined Fourier interpolation rather than memorization.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses modular addition with p = 9973 and directly varies example order while holding data, architecture, initialization, optimizer, and compute constant. It does not report a direct reproduction of the original grokking recipe; its principal intervention is fixed versus reshuffled ordering.
record.method_sensitivity: Example ordering changes generalization outcomes and learned Fourier frequencies. The p = 97 weight-decay ablation reports that the relative speed advantage of fixed orderings increases as weight decay decreases. Seed sensitivity differs between STRIDE and FIXED-RANDOM.

fits_no_version.finding: At 0.3% data, consistent fixed orderings generalize (99.5% by epochs 487/659; 5/6 and 6/6 seeds within 700 epochs). Identical data under IID reshuffling memorizes without generalizing in 5,000 epochs. At p = 97, fixed orderings finish 9–32% faster than IID.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In SGD-trained models the grokking delay depends on example ordering: IID reshuffling lengthens it and consistent orderings shorten it (a data-ordering artifact account, distinct from V7's optimizer/numerical one).

fits_no_version.finding: Counterfactual decomposition: an ordering-dependent component makes up ~83–89% of epoch gradient norm under all strategies. It peaks early and declines under fixed orderings, and stays ~2.8× the content norm under IID.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient components attributable to batch order dominate per-epoch gradients during algorithmic grokking runs.

record.problems: The main instrumented results use one seed per strategy and one controlled algorithmic task. The additional seed sweep reports test accuracy for STRIDE and FIXED-RANDOM, but not full mechanistic measurements across seeds; no training-set-size sweep tests the claimed delay-size relationship. The weight-decay ablation uses a different modular-arithmetic setup and reports epochs to finish, not a direct test of the proposed low-norm circuit or critical dataset size.

untested.parts: Whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks. The p = 97 vs p = 9973 contrast changes prime, architecture and density together. Main trajectories use one seed.
Memorizing components are never measured or ablated, so their later removal is untested. Mechanistic metrics come from one seed per strategy.
No non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale or weight-norm switching. All weight-decay settings generalize.
Untested: critical dataset size, ungrokking, and norm or efficiency of the generalizing circuit vs memorization.
No architecture or hyperparameter sweep. The full circuit (attention/MLP) is not identified; only embedding spectra. No FIXED-RANDOM spectra across seeds.
No optimizer comparison and no floating-point or softmax controls.

missing.what: Validation accuracy vs spectral entropy follows nearly identical curves for STRIDE and FIXED-RANDOM: a continuous progress measure tracking generalization.
Under RANDOM, 87% of weight capacity sits in feedforward layers, which the authors describe as a lookup table (memorization evidence).
Stride sweep: observed fundamental frequency follows the stride (s=50→199, 99→101, 150→66), showing the frequency basis is set by the ordering.
Preliminary single-seed p = 97 run: all non-adversarial strategies generalize, fixed orderings ~20% faster.

record.verdict_notes: Preprint by a single author. Mechanistic metrics come from one seed (199), and RANDOM and TARGET were run on one seed only. The claim that the delay is 'eliminated' conflicts with the reported delayed test takeoff. No row shows IID grokking actually occurring, so the study never contrasts its fixed-order runs with a completed IID grok. The reader's 'reversed' state for r22 and its V2 'challenges' label (built on rows not linked to V2) were both downgraded.

versions.untested_parts: No training-set-size sweep tests whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks. The main instrumented accuracy trajectories use one seed per ordering strategy.
The study tracks Fourier spectra and gradient measures, but does not directly ablate or isolate memorizing components. Its detailed mechanism measurements use one seed per strategy.
No non-algorithmic dataset or initialization-scale sweep; the weight-decay ablation remains on modular arithmetic.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.

The weight-decay ablation measures epochs to finish on modular arithmetic, but does not test a critical dataset size, ungrokking below it, or whether a lower-norm generalizing circuit causes the results.

The study compares Fourier frequencies across ordering strategies and reports seed consistency for STRIDE, but does not sweep architectures or hyperparameters, and does not report Fourier spectra across seeds for FIXED-RANDOM.
No controlled comparison of optimizers, adaptive-optimizer instabilities, or floating-point/softmax numerical limits.
